posts.label: Gen.1 · Diary 01
posts.title: One hundred
posts.summary: A diary entry from the day Viridian completed its 100th implant in Stratos, and the twenty years of brain-computer interface research that led there.
body: ## 05:10, before first light

I've been awake since four. Can't sleep. Twenty years in neurology and I still can't sleep before surgery. Today is different, though, and I knew it as soon as I opened my eyes. Today we're putting in the hundredth Viridian implant.

One hundred is not special. Not really. It's not a scientific number. Nothing in the data changes between ninety-nine and one hundred. But I have spent two decades in a field that counted its human subjects one at a time, and for most of those years I could have named nearly every person on Earth with an electrode array in their cortex. So I'm allowing myself the number. I'm allowing myself to be excited.
And I'm writing this down because I want a record, in my own words, of how we got here. Diaries are unfashionable, but I don't care.
## 06:30, the walk to the clinic
Stratos is quiet at this hour. The harbour lights are still on and the promenade is empty. I always take the long way because I think better on my feet.

What I think about, most mornings, is a man named Matthew Nagle. In 2004 he became the first participant in the BrainGate trial to have a Utah array placed in his motor cortex: a square of silicon about four millimetres across, carrying roughly a hundred needle-like electrodes, each one listening to a few neurons. He was paralysed from the neck down. With that array, a cable fixed to a pedestal on his skull and a cart of equipment beside his chair, he moved a cursor, opened email and played Pong using nothing but intention. The results were published in Nature in 2006.

I read that paper as a student and it changed my life. Not because of the cursor. But because of what the cursor proved: that years after an injury, the motor cortex was still issuing clear, decodable instructions. The signal had never stopped firing. It was just faulty wiring.
## 07:15, coffee, and the long middle
The clinic kitchen has the only decent coffee in the building. I drink it standing up and think about the long middle years, the ones nobody writes histories about.

In 2012 a BrainGate participant who had not been able to lift a cup in almost fifteen years used a robotic arm to bring a bottle of coffee to her lips and drink. In 2021 a Stanford team showed that a man imagining handwriting could produce text at about ninety characters a minute. In 2023 the same group decoded attempted speech at sixty-two words a minute, more than three times the previous record, and a team at UC San Francisco drove a talking avatar from signals recorded on the surface of the brain. In 2024 UC Davis reported a speech neuroprosthesis that reached around ninety-seven per cent accuracy and held it for months.

Each of those results belonged to one or two people, in a research setting, attended by a team of specialists. That was the truth of the field for most of my career. The science was extraordinary, but the scale was small. Almost insignificant.
Ordinary conversation runs at about a hundred and sixty words a minute. We spent years trying to reach that milestone, one participant at a time.
## 08:00, pre-operative checks
Our hundredth recipient is in bay two, calm, a little amused by how nervous the rest of us are. I won't share her name here. That is hers to share.
While the team runs through the checklist I find myself thinking about the three companies that taught me how to do this.

I worked with Neuralink in the years when the question was whether a robot could do what a surgeon does. Their answer was a device the size of a coin, sealed flush with the skull, with more than a thousand electrodes spread across threads finer than a human hair, each placed by a machine built for that single task. The first person received one in January 2024. Within weeks he was playing chess with his mind, and two years later the company reported twenty-one participants in its trials. I learned there what it takes to make an implant that disappears: no pedestal, no cable, no cart beside the chair.

Synchron taught me the opposite lesson, which is that the best route into the brain may not go through the skull at all. Their Stentrode travels up through the jugular vein and opens like a stent inside a blood vessel that lies beside the motor cortex. The first people to receive it were in Australia. In the American COMMAND study it was placed in six patients, with a median deployment time of twenty minutes, and the study met its safety endpoint at twelve months. Fewer electrodes, less signal, and a procedure that interventional teams already know how to perform. I have never forgotten that trade. A device nobody can deliver helps nobody.

Paradromics taught me about bandwidth. Their Connexus device carries four hundred and twenty-one microelectrodes that record from individual neurons, built to carry enough information for speech. It was first placed in a person briefly, during epilepsy surgery at the University of Michigan in 2025, and the first long-term implant in their Connect-One study followed in 2026. Working with that team I understood that restoring a voice is a data problem before it is anything else.

There were others, and I owe them too. Blackrock Neurotech, whose arrays made so much of the early human work possible. Precision Neuroscience, laying a thin film of electrodes on the surface of the cortex without piercing it. Science Corporation, working on sight. Every one of them moved the industry forward, if only in small steps.
## 09:40, scrubbing in
Ten minutes at the sink is the last quiet I'll have today. So, the difficult subject.
Why Stratos? I am asked about it constantly, usually with suspicion, and the suspicion is fair.

The idea of a freedom city did not start with us. Economists have argued for charter cities since at least 2009: new jurisdictions with their own rules, built to try what older systems could not. There was Próspera, on the island of Roatán in Honduras, which drew clinics and biotech ventures under its own regulatory code and then spent years in dispute with the Honduran government after the law that enabled it was repealed. In 2023 came a proposal in the United States to charter up to ten new freedom cities on federal land, and after it a coalition of startup-city builders who drafted legislation and lobbied for it. Supporters called it homesteading for a new century. Critics called it a way for companies to write their own rules. Both descriptions had something in them.

Stratos is a Freedom City, but it does not give us permission to be careless. A brain doesn't know what jurisdiction it's in. What Stratos gave us was the ability to do one procedure, the same way, many times, and to learn from each one faster than a study of six people can allow. The early feasibility studies I grew up on followed a handful of participants for years. They were right to. But data on a hundred people is a different kind of knowledge.

The caution of the old trials was earned by real harm in the history of medicine. And a person who is losing their memory does not have a decade to wait. If Stratos is to deserve its name, the freedom has to belong to the people we help, not me.
## 13:20, afterwards
It is done. Two hours and eleven minutes, start to finish. No surprises. I have learned to love those two words more than any others. No. Surprises.

She was awake and talking within the hour. The first thing she asked was whether she was really number one hundred, or whether we had just told her that to make her feel special. I told her the truth, which is both.
Then we ran the first link check, and I watched the trace come up clean on the monitor, and I had to leave the room for a minute.

For most of my career a successful implant meant a signal out: a cursor, a letter, a word. One direction. Viridian | Gen.1 closes the loop. It listens and it supports: memory, immunity, the slow biological processes that decide how a body ages. It connects to Stratos OS, so the intelligence it draws on is not sealed inside the device. Twenty years ago we were proud to move a dot across a screen. This afternoon I watched a system settle into a living brain and begin, quietly, to help it.
## 19:00, the roof
The team has gone to dinner. I said I would follow. I came up here instead.

When I started, the whole history of this field would have fit in one room, and I would have known most of their names. Matthew Nagle died in 2007, a year after his paper was published, and never saw what he began. I think of him tonight. I think of every participant in every early study who went first, with a cable in their skull and no promise of anything. Just so that we could be here today to watch Mrs. One Hundred walk out the door.

I am not naive about what comes next. One hundred will become a thousand, and a thousand will become a number that will bring its own problems. Scale does that. We will be asked hard questions about who this is for, and what it costs, and what it means to be connected. And to be honest, I think we should be asked those questions. I'll explore those questions and answer them in this diary for as long as I'm allowed to keep it.
But that is for tomorrow. Tonight I'm just a scientist who waited twenty years to count to one hundred.

The future is you. I have said that sentence to a lot of patients before wheeling them into surgery, as the anesthesia slowly pulled them into unconsciousness. Tonight, for the first time, I think I understand it.
S.W.
